US flew surveillance drone over Mexico to help capture top drug lord

Mexican officials say the United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help locate and capture one of the country's most wanted drug traffickers. The operation led to the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as 'El Chapo Isidro'.

Issued on: 24/11/2026 - 03:09

  2 min
Reading time
Share
By:
FRANCE 24
A Mexican National Guard helicopter flies overhead as soldiers stand guard during a security operation for the admission of drug lord "El Chapo Isidro" in Almoloya de Juarez, State of Mexico, on November 23, 2026. © Mario Vasquez, AFP

The United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa, Mexican security officials said Monday.

The recent detention of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro” illustrates increasing law enforcement cooperation between the neighboring countries, but U.S. involvement in Mexican security operations has long been a touchy subject.

U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to crack down on cartels, while Mexico has repeatedly underscored its sovereignty. On Monday, Sheinbaum emphasized that U.S. forces were not allowed to operate on the ground in Mexico and the governments were only sharing intelligence.

“This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces” of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said.

The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow them to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.

The weekend detention of the capo, who was one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, triggered a burst of violence in the northern state of Sinaloa that left 20 people dead in the city of Guasave. Among them were four soldiers and 16 suspected criminals, Mexican officials said Monday.

Defense Secretary Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said Monday that the capture of Meza Flores and 16 members of his criminal group was the result of “very important intelligence sharing” with U.S. authorities over the past three months to pinpoint Meza Flores’ location in Guasave.

In the week leading up to Meza Flores’ capture, that included authorizing the U.S. to fly intelligence drones over Mexican territory, to assist Mexican law enforcement to later surround the capo and go in for the capture, Trevilla Trejo and other Mexican officials said. They emphasized that the intelligence mission was carried out in compliance with Mexican law.

Authorities also noted on Monday that the U.S. had an existing extradition request for Meza Flores for drug trafficking charges, leaving open the possibility that the cartel boss may be sent north to face justice.

His capture was celebrated by Mexican and U.S. law enforcement as a major blow to criminal groups in the region.

The U.S. government highlighted its intelligence support in the operation, but did not immediately provide more details about the use of the surveillance drone when asked on Monday.

Meza Flores led the Beltran Leyva organization and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. He was also a key ally of a Sinaloa Cartel faction known as “Los Mayos," which is locked in a brutal territorial war against another cartel faction in the Mexican state.

The capture of Meza Flores was the latest in a string of targeted operations against cartel kingpins by Mexican authorities, the largest of which was the February killing of Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes , known as " El Mencho ."

While the captures show that the government is doubling down on its fight on crime, many experts were quick to emphasize that the strategy could backfire.

In previous anti-crime offensives in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, knocking out cartel leaders without debilitating the entire criminal structure around them has largely only fueled bloody power struggles between cartel factions. That has been the case in recent years in Sinaloa.

(FRANCE 24 with AP)

sources.headline: Capture of drug lord on FBI's most wanted list leads to more arrests
sources.text:
Updated on: November 23, 2026 / 11:37 AM EST
/ CBS/AFP
Add CBS News on Google
Eight suspected members of a gang led by Fausto Isidro Meza Flores have been arrested, Mexico's defense ministry said Sunday, after widespread violence swept across Sinaloa following the drug kingpin's capture. Meza Flores, alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured on Friday in the northwestern state during a special forces raid in coordination with U.S. intelligence. The military operation sparked panic in Guasave, sending civilians fleeing from erupting gunfire. Elsewhere in the state, suspected gang members reportedly erected improvised roadblocks.In clashes with security forces, 16 cartel suspects have been killed since the operation began, Defense Secretary Ricardo Trevilla said Monday. Four soldiers also died. The fresh arrests took place during a patrol by special forces who "were fired upon by members of a criminal group" linked to Chapo Isidro, Mexico's defense ministry posted on X. The ministry included a short video showing special forces arresting suspects at night. "In repelling the attack, they arrested eight members of the 'Beltran Leyva' criminal organization ... including one minor, who had participated in the roadblocks on November 20," the ministry's post said.The military also seized several high-caliber weapons and six vehicles, two of which had "improvised armor and a turret for mounting machine guns."
Chapo Isidro, 44, led a drug trafficking organization affiliated with the Beltran Leyva gang and allied with one of two rival factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel, according to U.S. and Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured on Friday in the northwestern state during a special forces raid in coordination with U.S. intelligence.
Mexico Government
He faces criminal charges in both Mexico and the United States. The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. On Saturday, the U.S. Justice Department called him a senior leader of the Sinaloa cartel, which it calls "one of the most prolific and dangerous drug cartels in Mexico, known for its widespread use of corruption and violence to further its drug trafficking activities." The Mexican defense ministry released dramatic video of the suspects being apprehended and escorted on to a military plane.
U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson said on X that "strategic intelligence sharing" between the U.S. and Mexico "helped make this operation possible."In a social media post Saturday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that Meza Flores had been captured "in an operation by the Mexican government supported by a coordinated interagency effort that included" the U.S. Homeland Security Task Force.
This undated image released by the U.S. Department of State shows Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
U.S. Department of State via AP
Chapo Isidro's capture came just days after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum met President Trump on the sidelines of a summit in Asia.Mr. Trump, who has pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said Friday that the two had discussed trade and security.The Mexican government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader, known as "El Mencho," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote in a post on X Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in the state of Sinaloa to protect civilians.

sources.headline: Explainer-Mexico nabs yet another top drug lord, but history of 'Kingpin Strategy' mixed
sources.text: MONTERREY, Mexico, Nov 23 - Mexico notched yet another victory in its intensifying anti-cartel war after elite soldiers nabbed one of the country's most wanted suspected narcos, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as Chapo Isidro, with intelligence help from Washington.Chapo Isidro was considered one of the leaders of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, a former ally of the powerful Sinaloa Cartel that later became one of its top rivals.His capture is the latest in a string of arrests of high-profile suspected drug traffickers as Mexico — under intense pressure from US President Donald Trump — has decisively returned to the so-called Kingpin Strategy.This approach was pioneered by US anti-drug officials working with the Colombian military to combat the Medellin and Cali cartels in the 1990s. The idea is to capture or kill the top leadership of powerful cartels in efforts to break them into smaller and weaker groups.But history has shown that this strategy can have unintended consequences. Power vacuums can spark bloody turf wars. And new groups spur new alliances that keep crime groups powerful enough to defy US and Mexican law enforcement.The focus of the US and Mexico’s renewed Kingpin Strategy has been the Sinaloa Cartel, one of Mexico’s two largest criminal groups. But the task is not easy. Here’s how the killing and capture of some of Mexico’s most high-profile narcos have realigned power within the Sinaloa Cartel over the last two decades — and how innocent civilians have gotten caught in the crossfire.THE BROTHERIn 2008, Mexican forces arrested Alfredo Beltrán Leyva in Sinaloa. At the time, he and his brothers were a key part of the Sinaloa Cartel’s drug trafficking and money laundering operations. But the arrest sparked suspicions that Sinaloa Cartel co-founder Joaquin Guzman Loera, better known as El Chapo, had betrayed Beltrán Leyva — kicking off a brutal rivalry between Alfredo’s brothers and El Chapo.At the time, Chapo Isidro sided with the Beltrán Leyva brothers, whose group came to be known as the Beltran Leyva Organization (BLO).The bitter war between Sinaloa and BLO provoked carnage across northern Mexico. In search of new allies, BLO partnered with the Juarez Cartel and Los Zetas against Sinaloa. The epicenter of the ensuing battle was Ciudad Juarez, which became one of the most dangerous cities in the world.THE KING OF CRYSTALIn 2010, Mexican soldiers shot dead Ignacio Coronel Villarreal in Jalisco (Mexican authorities said Coronel opened fire first). Known as Nacho Coronel or the "King of Crystal", he ruled over the Sinaloa Cartel’s methamphetamine production in western Mexico in alliance with the Milenio Cartel, according to US authorities.His death opened a chasm in Mexico’s criminal world that still reverberates today: some of Nacho Coronel’s top lieutenants broke off and formed a new crime group. One of them was Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as "El Mencho," who went on to form the hyperviolent mega cartel Jalisco New Generation, known as CJNG. Mexican forces killed El Mencho in an operation in February. But his group continues to terrorize civilians across Mexico.THE KINGPIN OF ALL KINGPINSIn 2016, Mexican soldiers recaptured El Chapo in Sinaloa — six months after he escaped from a maximum-security federal prison through an underground tunnel. He was a principal leader of the Sinaloa Cartel, authorities said, overseeing a multinational trafficking network that smuggled hundreds of tons of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine, and marijuana into the United States.His recapture and 2017 extradition to the US created a leadership vacuum within the cartel. After an internal dispute, El Chapo’s sons, known as "Los Chapitos," seized power.Unlike their father, who had presided over a drug trafficking empire dedicated to the traditional drugs at the time, they pioneered the Mexican production of an emerging new product: fentanyl. US law enforcement says their group oversaw the industrial manufacture and trafficking of the synthetic opioid, which killed tens of thousands of people a year.THE BETRAYALIn July 2024, US federal agents arrested Sinaloa Cartel co-founder Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada after he landed at a US airstrip near El Paso, Texas, on a private plane. Also on board: Joaquín Guzmán López, one of El Chapo’s sons, who according to US authorities and Zambada’s lawyer had lured the Sinaloa Cartel’s aging patriarch to a meeting under false pretenses and then forcibly flew him across the border to surrender him to US authorities.The alleged betrayal shattered the decades-long alliance between the Guzmán and Zambada families, plunging Sinaloa into a bloody turf war between "Los Chapitos" and Zambada’s loyalists, known as "Los Mayos."Before his arrest on Friday, Chapo Isidro had reportedly aligned with the Los Mayos faction. Security analysts say his removal could further destabilize the ongoing conflict, which has already left hundreds dead or missing and paralyzed daily life across parts of Sinaloa. REUTERS

sources.headline: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
sources.text: A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said. Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa.Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash.The US Consulate General in the city of Hermosillo said it was "monitoring reports of ongoing security operations, armed clashes, road blockades, and vehicle fires that occurred overnight in Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave, and Navolato" following the arrest of Meza-Flores.  It advised US citizens to remain alert for potential violence in the area and for residents to remain sheltered in place.When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.

Alleged Mexican drug cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro’ arrested in special forces raid

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade

Donna Ferguson
Sat 21 Nov 2026 12.46 EST
Share
Prefer the Guardian on Google

The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.

The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.

0:58
Vehicles burn on Mexican highway after capture of 'El Chapo Isidro' – video

His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.

Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.

The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.

Video posted by Mexican authorities shows police leading man away

After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.

The men were then evacuated to Mexico City on a Mexican air force plane to be handed over to prosecutors.

Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.

A barrage of rapid fire from what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters hit the ground, according to CNN, and players from the Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams abandoned the field mid-game.

Four Mexican army infantry soldiers died in the operation, the defence ministry said in a statement posted on X that extended the institution’s condolences to their families.

It added that security forces killed seven attackers and arrested eight alleged criminals in the operation, including three who were transferred to Mexico City and five who were turned over to the attorney general’s office in Culiacán, Sinaloa.

View image in fullscreen
Meza Flores’s FBI ‘most wanted’ poster. Photograph: FBI

Overnight on Friday the ​military operation triggered a wave of violence in the state of Sinaloa, including armed ‌clashes between Mexican security forces and cartel members, who ‌set up flaming roadblocks in some areas.

By ​Saturday the violence had substantially subsided. Sinaloa state authorities ​said “the situation is under control and being addressed by all levels of government”.

Meza Flores was originally indicted in 2012, and in 2013 the US Treasury placed sanctions on him under the Kingpin Act, freezing his assets.

In 2017, the US Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program began offering up to $5m as a reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.

He has been charged with multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations, and use and possession of a firearm in the US, and was wanted in Mexico for organised crime and offences against public health.

sources.headline: Mexican special forces arrest drug kingpin 'Chapo Isidro'
sources.text:
A gun battle between Mexican soldiers and alleged gang members in the city of Guasave, in the state of Sinaloa, ended with special forces detaining senior members of the Beltran Leyva drug trafficking network, Mexican officials said on Saturday.
The gang is aligned with the Mayos, one of the factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel.
Authorities said the overnight raid resulted in the capture of the suspected drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza F., better known as "Chapo Isidro," who is believed to be the leader of Beltran Leyva.
The operation left at least 11 people dead. Seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed, Mexico’s Defense Ministry said on Saturday afternoon.
FBI offering millions for 'Chapo Isidro'
The 44-year-old Mexican national is one of the FBI's ten most wanted fugitives. The US law enforcement agency claims his group is responsible for smuggling "large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States," and has offered a $5 million (€4.56 million) reward for information leading to his arrest.
He is also wanted in Mexico on charges including organized crime. "Chapo Isidro" was once a rival of imprisoned drug kingpin Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman.
The three detainees were transported to Mexico City "to be placed at the disposal of the competent prosecutorial authorities," the military said.
It was not immediately clear whether authorities would extradite "Chapo Isidro" to the US.
On Saturday, Mexican authorities said the raid was conducted due to "intelligence coordination" between Mexico's military and US agencies. However, they offered few details about how authorities in both countries coordinated.
In a post on X, US Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson wrote: "Results like these are not achieved overnight. They are the product of sustained cooperation and trust. This is what we can accomplish when we work together. ​We will continue pursuing criminals."Roads blocked in Sinaloa
The troops used "stealth and surprise" to reach the area, establishing a perimeter around the drug dealer's location and then moving in from multiple directions, according to Mexico's US embassy.
Unverified videos from Guasave, however, showed military helicopters firing at ground targets and sports fans scrambling for safety during a baseball game. Some of the violence in the western Mexican city seems to have taken place after "Chapo Isidro" was arrested, with drug cartels attempting to retaliate against the authorities and civilians for the move.
The military said security forces were deployed to restore traffic on roads and highways in Mexico's SinaloaImage: Yohari Leon/REUTERS
Mexico's Defense Ministry confirmed cartel members set up roadblocks in the area, but added that security forces were assisting local authorities in restoring order.
The Guasave raid is only the latest in a string of high-profile moves against senior leaders of Mexico's illegal drug trade​​​​​​. Less than two weeks ago, the Mexican Navy announced the arrest of Rafael A., suspected of leading a cartel cell active in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan.
Mexican President ​Claudia Sheinbaum is facing pressure from Donald Trump, who has threatened to take military action against cartels on Mexican territory.
Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

sources.headline: Cartel leader captured in northern Mexico in a bloody firefight that left 11 dead
sources.text:
FILE - Mexico's coat of arms decorates a large flag in Mexico City, on Nov. 13, 2025.
Claudia Rosel/AP
hide caption
Claudia Rosel/AP
GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — Heavy gunfire, helicopters and burning trucks marked Mexico's Sinaloa state Saturday after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," in an operation that left at least 11 people dead. Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after the firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized.
This undated image released by the U.S. Department of State shows Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores.
U.S. Department of State via AP
hide caption
U.S. Department of State via AP
Mexico's Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed. The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.
Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores. He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state. Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups. As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions. Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violenceThe capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city.
Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders. "The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city." Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities. Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case. "Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets. Terror in SinaloaGuasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations. "Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press. She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.
An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation. Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday. "The aftermath of last night's war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down," Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico. Guasave residents remained "very afraid" because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said. Capture prompts celebration and warningsMeza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office. The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities. "Results like these don't happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together," U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. "We will continue the hunt." Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa." Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February. Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run. The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.
"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

sources.text: An outburst of violence has killed at least 11 people after Mexican authorities captured suspected cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro.
